#ZeroDay #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
No CVE. No patch. And the exploit code is already public. 🪟

What The Hacker News reported (12 Nov):
→ A researcher known as MSNightmare posted SignDrop on GitHub on Patch Tuesday, proof-of-concept code that abuses the Windows CLFS driver (clfs.sys) to get local SYSTEM privileges
→ It targets the CLFS log authentication Microsoft added in October 2025 and uses the Defender antimalware service; Defender must be enabled for the chain to work
→ Tested on Windows 11 26H2 and Windows Server 2025 builds, per the repository
→ Microsoft has not confirmed the flaw, assigned a CVE or released a fix; it is not in CISA KEV and no attacks have been reported
→ 78researchlab confirmed the exploit works but judged it not reliable enough for real operations

What to do: check the CLFS Authentication mode on your Windows builds, don't switch the mitigation off (modes 2 or 3 let CLFS parse tampered logs), watch the MSRC update guide, and alert on odd behaviour from low-privilege accounts. Three of this researcher's earlier Defender flaws have been exploited in attacks, per The Hacker News.

cover.hook: 35,578 Grok-built apps open to anyone. Some leaking passwords.
cover.sub: Researchers say "Anyone with the link" was preselected when they built an app.

slides.title: What researchers found
slides.body: Claroc found 37,571 apps built with Grok. 35,578 could be opened without signing in. About 1 in 10 open apps held internal business or personal data, and roughly 2% were rated high or critical.

slides.title: Whose data
slides.body: Internal data from 30 other organizations turned up, per the researchers: 26 with more than 1,000 employees and 6 in the Fortune 500. 24 apps were built by staff at X and SpaceXSI.

slides.label: Grok-built apps reachable without sign-in
slides.note: Out of 37,571 found. Claroc research, via The Hacker News (11 Nov)

slides.title: The response
slides.body: SpaceXSI (formerly xAI) took down the 24 staff apps and says apps stay private until shared. Claroc says the setting was preselected on the paid account it used, and asks for "Only you" as the default.

slides.title: Do this week
items: Find apps your staff built with AI app builders
Set internal apps to Invited users or Only you
Check app scripts for hard-coded passwords and keys

segments.show: Huntress says attackers used ScreenConnect's Run Command feature to push rogue ScreenConnect clients to at least 288 managed endpoints across 48 organizations. First detected 11 Nov.

segments.say: Huntress sees no new bug. Likely stolen logins or hijacked sessions. ConnectWise switched off five add-ons.
segments.show: Huntress: likely compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions. ConnectWise disabled five third-party extensions (RMM Plus family); about 400 partner environments had one installed. It says there's no evidence of a ScreenConnect vulnerability.

segments.say: Check your Run Command history today, even if nothing alerted.
segments.show: Hunt for unusual sign-ins, new admin accounts, unexpected extensions or commands, and unapproved remote tools. Developing story. Source: The Hacker News, 12 Nov.

→ Huntress says attackers used ScreenConnect's Run Command feature to push rogue ScreenConnect clients to at least 288 managed endpoints across 48 organizations, first detected on 11 Nov
→ Huntress has seen no evidence of a new vulnerability; it says initial access was likely compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions
→ Huntress says the MSPs were tagged with sequential numbers, so others may have been hit earlier

Do today: review Run Command history even if nothing alerted, hunt for unusual sign-ins, new admin accounts, unexpected extensions and unapproved remote-access software, and preserve logs of anything suspicious.

cover.hook: An AI pentest platform. Linked to attacks that read AWS production secrets.
cover.sub: Arctic Wolf says systems hosting AntiFox were tied to confirmed malicious actions.

slides.title: What it is
slides.body: AntiFox is described as an AI-driven autonomous penetration testing platform, downloadable from GitHub and built on ARTEX, another AI pentest tool. Its multi-agent system runs recon, discovery, exploitation and reporting.

slides.title: What Arctic Wolf saw
slides.body: Arctic Wolf Labs says Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions: web exploitation, a web shell, then cloud enumeration. In some cases a GetSecretValue call succeeded against a production secret.

slides.label: hosts running an exposed ARTEX console (Censys, 4 Nov)
slides.note: Check Point counted 2,557 systems that hosted ARTEX. Via The Hacker News (11 Nov)

slides.title: What's still unknown
slides.body: The exact vulnerability used to run code on the IIS server isn't known, and no intrusion dates are given. Not every exposed ARTEX instance is necessarily malicious, the article notes.

slides.title: Do this week
items: Limit which roles can read production secrets
Keep secrets out of web server configs
Patch and monitor internet-facing IIS servers
